MEMORANDUM OF LAW

TO: Partner; Legal Writing Fellow
FROM: Associate
DATE: September 22, 2026
RE: Doe; Dwelling definition under FHA

Discussion

Doe can only pursue a cause of action for violations of the Fair Housing Act if the apartment he leased from Residence Co. would be considered a dwelling under the Act. For the purposes of defining a dwelling under the FHA, the applicable statutory definition is 42 U.S. Code § 3602 (b):

“Dwelling” means any building, structure, or portion thereof which is occupied as, or designed or intended for occupancy as, a residence by one or more families, and any vacant land which is offered for sale or lease for the construction or location thereon of any such building, structure, or portion thereof. 42 U.S.C. § 3602(b).

It is worth noting that (c) of that section clarifies the definition of family:

"Family" includes a single individual. 42 U.S.C. § 3602(c).The key term over which the plain text of the statute does not provide a clear definition is “residence”. Instead, we must look to the Third Circuits’ two-part test first proffered in Columbus Country Club and then clarified in Lakeside Resort Enterprises to determine what meets the threshold:

“First, we must decide whether the facility is ‘intended or designed’ for occupants who ‘intend to remain in the [facility] for any significant period of time.’ 915 F.2d at 881. Second, we must determine whether those occupants would ‘view [the facility] as a place to return to’ during that period.” Lakeside Resort Enters., LP v. Bd. of Supervisors of Palmyra Twp., 455 F.3d 154, 158 (3d Cir. 2006) (quoting United States v. Columbus Country Club, 915 F.2d 877, 881 (3d Cir. 1990))

I. The Residence Co. facility was ‘intended or designed’ for Doe to remain in for a ‘significant period of time’

To an individual plaintiff bringing a case under the FHA, “It is the period the [facility] was intended or designed to be available to him that is relevant, not the amount of time the [facility] may have been available to others.” Smith v. Salvation Army, No. 13-114-J, (W.D. Pa. 2015). For the purposes of Doe’ claim, it is highly likely that Residence Co. would meet the first part of the test. Doe did not remain at Residence Co. for more than 4 weeks, but he had the option to stay for the facilities’ maximum term of 4 months.

Courts “have not defined what is a "significant period of time" other than to say that (1) five months is significant, id., and (2) "for the rest of [the occupants'] lives" is significant, Hovsons, 89 F.3d at 1102.” Lakeside, 455 F.3d at 159 While 4 weeks seems well below both those figures, the maximum term of 4 months is more relevant. Lakeside clarified that “Congress did not, by its words, require only that a facility be "occupied as" a residence. Thus, that health-insurance funding limits some residents to 14.8 days or less does not itself deprive the … facility of its residential status.” Lakeside, 455 F.3d at 159. given that a facility “is intended to accommodate 30-day stays as a matter of course and even longer stays on occasion.”. Lakeside, 455 F.3d at 159. leading the Third Circuit to find that “In this context, we conclude that the 14.8-day average stay at the proposed facility is more nuanced than perceived at first blush, and qualifies that facility under the first factor of Columbus Country Club” Lakeside, 455 F.3d at 159.

Doe' actual stay at Residence Co. was double the average in Lakeside, and the stay available to him was 4 months, far beyond the common 30-day stays and well into the “even longer” territory contemplated by that case. To him, therefore, Residence Co. was ‘intended or designed’ for him to remain for a ‘significant period of time’ and meets the first part of the test.

II. Doe would most likely ‘view [the facility] as a place to return to’ by the standards of applicable case law

In Columbus Country Club the Third Circuit found that members’ bungalows qualified as a residence not only on the question of duration but also that they treated it as a residence; “the country club's members saw their individual bungalows as homes. The members repeatedly returned to the same bungalow because they felt at home there.10 Similarly, we noted in Hovsons that, " [t]o the handicapped elderly persons who would reside there, [the nursing facility] would be their home, very often for the rest of their lives." Lakeside, 455 F.3d at 159.

Looking at the qualitative attributes of Residence Co., it is likely that it meets this test as well based on the overlap of features from relevant cases. Residence Co. gives residents “access to a communal kitchen, communal bathrooms, an office space where they can work, a commons area where they can gather and socialize with other residents and host visitors, and a mailroom where they can receive packages.” this closely mirrors the Lakeside case where “residents would eat meals together (separated by gender), return to their rooms in the evening, receive mail at the facility, and make it their "residence" while they were there.” Lakeside, 455 F.3d at 159–60. Residence Co. is slightly short of Lakeside in two respects. Guests can be hosted in the common area, but not necessarily in residents’ rooms (need to confirm with client), and rooms can be decorated, but nails cannot be driven into the wall. It makes up for it in other aspects, however, in that residents can come and go as they please and have their own keys.

District courts have allowed cases to proceed with a much lower standard than Lakeside. Even in cases where residents have “a highly regimented schedule in which residents are required to have group meeting and attend church services, and residents do not have individual rooms and are not allowed to personalize or decorate their sleeping space” DeFiore v. City Rescue Mission of New Castle, 995 F. Supp. 2d 413, 418–19 (W.D. Pa. 2013)., the court found it could still qualify given “the fact that residents receive mail at Crossroads; that residents have medication dispensed by Crossroads staff; and that residents return to their sleeping areas in the evening.” DeFiore, 995 F. Supp. 2d at 418–19. Residence Co. is well above this standard given the residents have individual rooms, freedom to come and go, and are permitted to customize their rooms, absent the use of nails.

Given that Residence Co. matches the Lakeside standard in most respects and exceeds it in some while being well clear of the lower DeFiore standard in virtually every way, it is likely that the ‘place to return to’ standard is met here.

Conclusion

Under the relevant two-part standard that courts have adopted for the threshold of dwelling, it is highly likely that Doe's case can meet the standard. The first and quantitative component should be easily met with high confidence given his actual and potential stay well exceeds the reference figures in Lakeside. The second and qualitative component is more uncertain, given its more subjective nature as well as the relevant facts in this case. Even so, it is very similar to the bar cleared in Lakeside and well above that in DeFiore. While we cannot say for certain that the court will find it above the mark, it is highly likely that it does. As far as Doe is concerned, Residence Co. is highly likely to meet both components of the two-part test and therefore be considered a dwelling for his case.
